rv.q: Rachel O’Riordan’s sensitive production is not afraid to take its time and sit in its silences, allowing ruminative rhythms to play out.
That’s what makes this play beautiful: in defiance of its own title, it’s about what endures.
Though both kind and astute, this is the most awkward play in the trilogy: an uneasy mixture of detail and declamation.
O’Riordan handles the sensitive, slow-paced piece with great finesse, assuredly judging when to let a pause stretch into a loaded silence and when to slip in an uplifting moment of humour.
This kind of nicely observed writing needs fabulous playing to stop from feeling like nicely observed writing.
But Alfie and Julie’s dialogue and actions often feel wildly implausible in the context of a 90-minute realtime conversation, overly crammed with exposition and incident.

Sometimes the dialogue gives way to monologues on life and death that sit oddly against the domestic realism (the kitchen set, containing vinyl and an acid house smiley face clock, is designed by Gary McCann).
End works beautiful on all counts.

The entire triptych is a considerable achievement, an assertion of Alfie’s final sense that music and art have meaning by “creating fleeting moments of joy in this dark, f*cked-up world” and of Julie’s that writing can make sense of the universe.
Such perfect performances prove that this is an outstanding way of finishing a trilogy which encompasses all of life.
Owen and Reeves, at the top of their game, make the battle for a good death heartbreakingly poignant and fragile.
Overall, a thoughtful and poignant experience.
End falters in its reluctance to push further than gentle inquiry.
O'Riordan's sensitive, subtle production is the final show programmed by the National's former artistic director Rufus Norris, a mixed reign ending on a high.

cn.t: Eldridge's trilogy concludes with a tender, quietly moving two-hander about a couple facing terminal illness, though critics are divided on whether its emotional restraint feels poignant or overly sentimental.
